title: Factored Verification: Detecting and Reducing Hallucination in Summaries of Academic Papers
abstract: Hallucination plagues even frontier LLMsbut how bad is it really for summarizing academic papers?We evaluate Factored Verification, a simple automated method for detecting hallucinations in abstractive summaries.This method sets a new SotA on hallucination detection in the summarization task of the HaluEval benchmark, achieving 76.2% accuracy.We then use this method to estimate how often language models hallucinate when summarizing across multiple academic papers and find 0.62 hallucinations in the average ChatGPT (16k) summary, 0.84 for GPT-4, and 1.55 for Claude 2. We ask models to self-correct using factored critiques and find that this lowers the number of hallucinations to 0.49 for ChatGPT, 0.46 for GPT-4, and 0.95 for Claude 2. The hallucinations we find are often subtle, so we advise caution when using models to synthesize academic papers.

claims.text: Factored Verification achieves 76.2% accuracy on the summarization task of the HaluEval benchmark.
Factored Verification exceeds the previous chain-of-thought method on HaluEval summarization by 10 absolute percentage points using the same language model.
ChatGPT (16k) produces an estimated average of 0.62 hallucinations per summary when summarizing scientific paper abstracts.
GPT-4 produces an estimated average of 0.84 hallucinations per summary when summarizing scientific paper abstracts.
Claude 2 produces an estimated average of 1.55 hallucinations per summary when summarizing scientific paper abstracts.
Self-correction using factored critiques reduces the estimated average number of hallucinations in ChatGPT summaries to 0.49.
Self-correction using factored critiques reduces the estimated average number of hallucinations in GPT-4 summaries to 0.46.
Self-correction using factored critiques reduces the estimated average number of hallucinations in Claude 2 summaries to 0.95.
Asking GPT-4 to directly self-correct without factored critiques increases the average number of detected hallucinations from 1.55 to 2.13.

limitations.text: Hallucination remains a largely unsolved problem for LLMs when applied to tasks requiring high factual accuracy such as scientific summarization.
Direct LLM self-correction without external structure struggles and can increase errors across reasoning datasets.
Automated evaluation via Factored Verification exhibits false positives and false negatives, agreeing with human judgments on unsupported claims only 66% of the time.
Significant hallucination rates persist in state-of-the-art LLM summaries even after self-correcting with factored critiques (0.46 to 1.24 estimated hallucinations per summary).
HaluEval evaluation was constrained to a random 5% training sample and 20% test sample due to compute cost limitations.
Non-expert human contractors showed low inter-rater agreement (38%) when attempting to evaluate unsupported academic claims.

future_work.text: Finetune language models on model-revised summaries to incrementally bootstrap more accurate summaries.
Extend factored critique approaches beyond hallucination reduction to richer tasks for scalable oversight.

methodologies.name: Factored Verification
methodologies.description: An automated method that decomposes summaries into atomic sentence-level claims, evaluates each claim against source text using LLM critiques, concatenates negative critiques into feedback, and prompts the LLM to revise the summary.
